extracted.intended_audience: literary scholars, students, and readers of 18th-century periodical essays
extracted.subtask_description: Critical commentary and prescriptive remarks about theatre, poetry, conversation, and satire as found in early-18th-century periodical essays (Spectator/Tatler-style). Focuses on what constitutes good drama, polite conversation, poetic diction, and satirical method.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simplicity of behaviour as perfection
rubrics_metrics.description: "simplicity of behaviour, which is the perfection of good breeding and good sense"
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Simplicity in behaviour and conversation is presented as the ideal of good breeding and sound sense; the essay laments that this quality is 'utterly lost in the world' and replaced by affectations and impostures. Use natural, plain behaviour to demonstrate wit and good sense rather than artificial refinements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid the 'Biter' / sneerer anti-pattern
rubrics_metrics.description: Definition and critique: "A Biter is one who tells you a thing you have no reason to disbelieve in itself... and if you give him credit, laughs in your face, and triumphs that he has deceived you."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat biting (telling plausible falsehoods with the intent to mock) as a social vice and aesthetic defect. Conversational wit should not be built on deceitful trickery or mean-spirited exposure; avoid cultivating the biter's habit of triumphing over those who trust him.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theatre must have wit, spirit, humour, and good sense
rubrics_metrics.description: "Wit and spirit, humour and good sense" are required qualities for the revival and health of the stage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The essay argues that genuine dramatic theatre depends on these qualities rather than on spectacles or low entertainments. Plays and performers should prioritise intelligent humour and moral/ethical sense in their writing and performance to influence manners positively.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theatre governance by competent judges
rubrics_metrics.description: "Wit and spirit... can never be revived, but under the government of those who are judges of such talents, who know, that whatever is put up in their stead, is but a short and trifling expedient"
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dramatic institutions should be directed or overseen by people who understand literary and theatrical talent; managerial or purely commercial control leads to inferior programming (spectacle over substance). Selection and organization of theatrical offerings should be entrusted to knowledgeable arbiters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid substituting spectacle for dramatic action
rubrics_metrics.description: Criticism of bringing in "ladder-dancers, rope-dancers, jugglers, and mountebanks" in place of Shakespeare's heroes and Jonson's humorists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not replace substantial dramatic action and character with acrobatic or purely visual entertainments. Preserve plot, character, and rhetorical depth instead of relying on song, dance, or mountebank amusements to fill the stage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Satire as social corrective: laugh out of countenance or promote opinions
rubrics_metrics.description: "This method is the same that was used by old Athenians, to laugh out of countenance, or promote opinions among the people."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use ridicule and comedic representation to expose follies and change public opinion. Satirical drama and essays should aim to shame or deflate vices and superstitions through humour and lampoon rather than mere insult.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetic diction and natural rhymes
rubrics_metrics.description: Authorial critique: "Avail and toil, defect and tract, will never do for rhymes."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In poetry, avoid forced or awkward rhymes and archaisms that jar the reader. Rhyme and diction should feel natural and suited to the subject; contrived pairings damage the verse's effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technique for exposing hypocrisy in satire
rubrics_metrics.description: Observation: "in company, very grave discourses have been followed by bawdry; and therefore has turned the humour that way with great success" (the playwright turns solemn discourse into bawdy to expose enthusiasm/hypocrisy).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A satirical tactic is to juxtapose high-sounding or solemn discourse with bawdy or hypocritical action to reveal the true character of the subjects. Employ contrast between professed piety/seriousness and actual behaviour to undermine pretence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid theatrical ostentation in representations of real death
rubrics_metrics.description: "None but a tragedian can die by rule... In real life, this is a chimera; and by noble spirits, it will be done decently, without the ostentation of it."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When portraying death or extreme emotion, prefer naturalness over contrived, 'by-rule' theatrical gestures. Realistic restraint is more noble and convincing than elaborate stagey displays when aiming for authenticity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conversational wit should be grounded in learning, reason, and experience
rubrics_metrics.description: Contrast: formerly 'a man of sense and free spirit... was built upon learning, reason, and experience' versus the modern 'impudent creature made up of vice only' who substitutes ignorance with contempt.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Valued conversational wit arises from education, reflection, and good sense. Avoid equating sham insolence or vice with genuine wit; cultivate informed, reasoned humour rather than bravado or affectation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of allegory/masque to represent political realities
rubrics_metrics.description: Description of a dance representing 'absolute power' (a tall man gives a kick down the line) and its inversion as a 'free state' where equals kick each other.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allegorical devices (dance, masque, tableau) can be effective stage tools to convey political commentary. When used, they should be clear in their moral/political intent and crafted to illuminate power relations rather than merely entertain.
